The only reason we stayed with them was because they’re one of the few places open on Saturdays and close relatively late on weekdays. But their system and inventory management? It’s like they’re stuck in the 1980s.

This week, my doctor prescribed penicillin—a basic, common antibiotic that’s been around since the 1920s—for a severe bacterial infection. I got a text saying my prescription was being prepared, so I waited in the parking lot for almost two hours. When I finally went inside to check, the front desk was dismissive and told me, without a hint of apology, that they were out of stock and I had to go speak to the pharmacist.

The pharmacist couldn’t have been more unhelpful or rude. She didn’t even look at the system before telling me to “just come back tomorrow.” At that point, I had a 104°F fever, could barely swallow, and was visibly in pain. I asked if she could at least check which medication was unavailable—my doctor had prescribed three. If penicillin was in stock, could I please get it for tonight?

Her response? “The more you talk, the slower I get,” followed by telling me her shift was ending soon. I stood there in silence while she reluctantly typed a few things into the system—and just like that, the prescription was suddenly ready. It wasn’t an insurance issue at all—my insurance was perfectly valid. The delay was entirely caused by Costco’s system or process failures.

This isn’t an isolated experience. Just a few days earlier, I waited nearly 90 minutes after getting a “ready” text for my baby’s liquid antibiotics—same disorganization, same cold attitude.

[{"content":"Been coming here for the last 2 years for my vaccines since usually their pharmacy staff to patient ratio is better than other places. In fact I drive 25 miles here & pay for the CPMC garage parking since if you don’t have a Sutter appt and just come here for Walgreens, they don’t reimburse parking. And they only open M-F. So you can tell this place meant a lot to me.

However the reason why I’m marking 1 star today is because their technician did not safely administer the flu vaccine. They inserted the vaccine in the wrong place. I know since I’m trained as a PharmD and an IM injection on the arm for a flu shot should be 2-3 fingers down form the top of the shoulder and in the thickest part of the deltoid, but above the armpit level. Too high, you risk bursitis - which could permanently impair raising your arm. Too low, you risk hitting the radial nerve that controls your arm and hands, and could also permanently impair use of your hand. And in this case where the pharmacy tech injected was off center and too far ventrally towards the chest, where you risk hitting the auxiliary nerve and impairing motor control as well.

Sadly, I didn’t realize the placement was off until I came home and saw in the mirror where my bruise was from the injection site after the bandage was taken off.

Honestly, it brings me no joy to leave negative reviews and to lose a pharmacy that I drive up 25 miles to especially since I thought with a better staff to patient ratio, they’d have more time/attention for each patient and less medication risks.

But I do draw the line at unsafe practices and health hazards. And also it really makes me question if technicians are ready for this responsibility. It used be only the pharmacist at the pharmacy (or your HCP if you want to use you medical insurance benefits instead of your PBM).

So I’m posting here more for public awareness.

But to be fair balanced, when the pharmacist gave me my Tdap vaccine the week before, the placement was ok. Manazah is highly experienced and very thorough but beyond that she is available at a moment’s notice to assist you with any questions. STAFF
Friendly, warm and kind. Always a nice greeting and the front office staff will work to make sure your needs are met. Never left endlessly on hold, never rude, always listening and accommodating. Staff seems consistent and low turnover which means they end up knowing the client well.
ENVIRONMENT
Bright, easy access to parking lot and on first floor so good for patients with disabilities. Offers wide variety of over the counter items but also a small gift shop with cards, jewelry, candles, lotion and skin care. This is what I call “a mom and pop” it is not a Rite Aide or Walgreens the office is located in a medical building and has a small reception area for waiting and two areas to check out. Wait time no longer than 5 to 10 minutes usually 5.
DELIVERY
Excellent, reliable and an affordable delivery fee. Same person delivers every day so I like that. Limited delivery areas so check the website.
ONLINE
Website is minimal but works for ordering your meds but not for communicating. Create profile and enter your prescription and good to go.
PARKING
This can be tricky because it is a large office building so competition for spots is real. I want to highly commend the team at this Walgreens pharmacy. The staff members are consistently helpful, patient, and friendly, whether answering questions over the phone or assisting me in person. Mobility & Seating Layout: During peak hours or pre-holiday surges, wait times naturally increase. I recently noticed a gentleman with a cane having to lean on a shopping cart for support. Unfortunately, the long security pole attached to the cart made it difficult for him to navigate over to the window seating area. Adding a few accessible chairs directly alongside the main queue line would safely accommodate elderly clients and those using assistive walking devices.

Front-Facing Staffing: Because insurance verifications are highly complex and time-consuming, lines can back up quickly. It would be incredibly helpful to have three dedicated team members at the front during peak times—allowing one or two to focus entirely on customer transactions while another expertly navigates insurance issues.

Live Phone Support: While automated AI systems serve a purpose, complex medication and insurance issues are often resolved much faster by a person. Dedicating more live-agent support on the pharmacy phone line would allow clients to resolve friction before arriving, significantly cutting down in-store wait times and boosting employee workflow.

[{"content":"I am the care coordinator for a medically complex disabled person. After Rite Aid closed, I transferred the prescriptions for the person I care for to Walgreens in Scotts Valley, following years of seamless, quality service at Rite Aid.

Then came Walgreens.

For an entire year, I dealt with medication delays, insurance problems, incomplete fills, endless holds, promised callbacks that never happened, and hours spent resolving problems the pharmacy should have been handling.

What was particularly astonishing was their inability to learn from previous mistakes. We would spend hours figuring out how to process a prescription, only to encounter the exact same problem the next time. It was as though nobody remembered anything from one prescription to the next.

The final straw came when another complicated prescription required additional troubleshooting. I asked the pharmacist to call Medi-Cal again to explore other options. Her response included, "I don't like wasting my time." She refused to make another call.

When I expressed my frustration with the pharmacy's consistently terrible service, the pharmacist became rude and combative, raised her voice, and actually told me that other people wouldn't agree with my assessment.

Really? This pharmacy has around two stars on multiple review platforms, with numerous customers describing similarly poor experiences. Apparently, quite a few people agree with me.

Rather than trying to resolve the problem, the pharmacist ultimately told me to take the prescriptions for the person I care for somewhere else. All of them!

So I did. And I transferred the prescriptions for four other people as well.

Think about that. A medically complex disabled person needed additional help obtaining medication, and the pharmacist decided she had spent enough time on the problem. Her solution was to send us elsewhere.

I cannot say whether this legally qualifies as discrimination, but I absolutely believe the treatment was discriminatory. When a disabled person's prescriptions require additional time and effort, refusing further troubleshooting, complaining about wasting time, and directing the caregiver elsewhere raises serious concerns about equal access to care.

That is not wasted time. That is part of providing pharmacy care.

Here's what makes this experience even more ridiculous.

I transferred everything to CVS in Scotts Valley, where the prescriptions have been filled with little to no difficulty or delay. CVS even had to correct an insurance issue Walgreens created by incorrectly processing a 30-day prescription as a 90-day prescription, preventing the person I care for from receiving her medication on time. CVS figured it out and fixed it.

What a difference!

If you coordinate care for someone with a disability, I would think very carefully before trusting Walgreens in Scotts Valley with their medications.

The last thing caregivers need is another job managing a pharmacy's incompetence.

I had a very poor experience trying to fill an asthma controller inhaler at this Walgreens. I had been out of my controller inhaler since around 6/11, contacted my provider on 6/17, and had prescriptions sent on 6/18, 6/23, and 7/3. Despite that, I still could not get the controller inhaler filled through this location.

To be clear, I have had prescriptions filled successfully here before. I am not saying every interaction at this pharmacy has been bad. The issue is how this specific asthma medication problem was handled once it became complicated.

Between 6/18 and 7/8, I went to the pharmacy in person three times and called once about the same unresolved issue. I was repeatedly told only some version of “we don’t have it” or “come back later.” That was not enough information.

“We don’t have it” could mean many different things: no prescription received, no physical stock, insurance rejection, early refill rejection, prior authorization, provider response needed, a pending refill request, or a stuck claim. Those are different problems requiring different next steps.

At one point, I was told the medication would be manually ordered and should arrive Monday. Monday came and I did not receive a clear update. Later, after pushing for more information, I was finally shown that one medication was out of stock, while another appeared to involve a provider/refill or insurance issue. Those should have been explained clearly much earlier.

There was also confusion around provider contact/fax information. If the pharmacy is waiting on a provider, patients need to know what was requested, when it was sent, and what specific response is needed.

Near closing, staff gave me a list of other Walgreens locations. That might help if the only issue is stock, but it does not solve insurance, early refill, prior authorization, provider-response, or claim problems.

I understand pharmacies are busy, medications can be delayed, and staff have closing procedures. But this was a medically important asthma controller medication, and I had already been without it for weeks while using albuterol daily. The problem was not just the delay. The problem was vague communication and poor exception handling.

[{"content":"It was complete mismanagement and chaos when I went to get my Covid and flu shots. I had scheduled an appointment for 2:00 PM the day before and arrived at 1:50 PM. There was a single long line for people dropping off prescriptions, picking up prescriptions, walk-ins for flu shots, and people with appointments.
When I tried to walk up to the counter (since I had a confirmed 2:00 PM appointment), people in the queue started shouting at me. I told them I had an appointment for my vaccination. Then the person at the counter shouted back, telling me that everyone stands in the same queue whether they have an appointment or are a walk-in. I asked him, "What is the use of making an appointment then?" To which he gave a ridiculous answer—he told me to ask Safeway that. Here I was, standing in a Safeway, and the staff at the Safeway counter was telling me to go ask Safeway! If that’s the case, I don't understand the point of having an appointment system at all. It reminded me of that Seinfeld episode where Jerry keeps insisting he reserved a rental car, but the person at the counter keeps saying they don't have a car held for him.
So, I stood in line. When my turn finally came, I gave all my information and asked the person helping me if they had the mRNA flu vaccine. She said yes, and I told her I would like to get that one. She assured me she would make sure I got that specific vaccine, so based on that promise, I signed the approval. By this point, it was already 20 minutes past my appointment time.
Next, I stood in line for the actual shot area, where there was more chaos and mismanagement. Someone who registered after me was called in for their shot before me. When I pointed this out, the staff member said they administer shots in the order they receive the paperwork.
When my turn finally came to take the shot, I reiterated my choice of the mRNA flu vaccine to the staff member. At that point, he told me, "We don't have that vaccine." I gave in and decided to take whatever flu vaccine they had. But then they said I would have to stand in line once again to reverse the transaction so my insurance wouldn't be charged for a shot I never received!
I finally decided to give up because it was already late, and I was going to be late for my next appointment.
This happened at Safeway, but I am sure the experience is the same whether you go to Walgreens, CVS, or another mega-corporation. What they are after is money and profit, and there is no real outlet for consumers to express their displeasure at being treated poorly. Vaccines are a lucrative business with high profit margins, and all these pharmacies want a piece of that profit without investing in more staff or upgrading their infrastructure to streamline the customer experience. All this Safeway or the nearby CVS cares about is profit. Customer satisfaction is not in their vocabulary. It is a race to the bottom, and CVS, Walgreens, Walmart, and Safeway all know that customer service everywhere is bad because consumers have no choice.
